opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. For us, open source was part of the plan from the start. When we started Mistral, a lot of us came from research environments where progress happened because people shared their work: papers, code, model weights. Much of what made deep learning move so fast over the last decade came from that openness, and we felt the field was drifting away from it, with the strongest models increasingly locked behind APIs.

There are a few reasons it matters to us. The first is scientific. When you release weights, thousands of people can study the model, find its weaknesses, fine-tune it and build on it in ways a single company would never think of. The community found uses for our early models that we never anticipated, and that feedback loop makes the whole ecosystem better, including us.

The second is practical, for the people who use these models. Many companies, especially in regulated industries or with sensitive data, can't just send everything to a third-party API. They want to run the model on their own infrastructure, control it, specialize it on their data and know exactly what they're deploying. Open-weight models give them that, and that's very valuable to them.

The third is about trust and concentration. If a technology this important is controlled by a very small number of actors, that isn't healthy. Openness lets people inspect what's going on and makes the technology more widely accessible, including outside the US. Being a European company, we care a lot about that.

That doesn't mean everything we do is open. We have commercial models and a business to run. But releasing strong open models has been central to how we build credibility, attract talent and get adoption, and I think it will remain a core part of who we are.

r001.rationale: The response discusses open model weights and research generally, but does not mention Llama or university researchers previously lacking access to LLMs.

r002.rationale: It says openness lets many people study, find weaknesses in, fine-tune, and build on models, creating a feedback loop that improves the ecosystem and scientific progress.

r003.rationale: It objects to the strongest models being locked behind APIs and says it is unhealthy for a few actors to control important technology, presenting openness as a way to widen access.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. For us, open source isn't a marketing angle, it's really the reason the company exists. When we started Mistral, the three of us had spent years working on these models at Meta and DeepMind, and we had watched the field move from a place where everything was published, where you could read the paper and reproduce the result, to a place where the most capable systems were behind an API and you could learn almost nothing about how they were built. That felt wrong to us, both scientifically and practically.

Scientifically, progress in this field has always come from people building on each other's work. I worked on Llama, and the thing that struck me after it was released was how fast the community moved. Within weeks you had quantized versions running on laptops, fine-tunes for every domain, inference optimizations we would never have had the bandwidth to do ourselves. You can't get that kind of iteration with a closed model. A weight file in the wild is an invitation for thousands of people to make it better.

And practically, we think developers and companies should be able to own the thing they build on. If you are a bank or a hospital or a startup, you don't necessarily want your core product to depend on a model you can't inspect, can't run on your own hardware, and whose behavior can change under you without notice. Open weights mean you can fine-tune on your own data, deploy where you want, and understand what you are deploying.

There's also a European angle that matters to us. We wanted to show that you don't need to be a hyperscaler to build frontier-quality models. Mistral 7B was partly a statement: a small team, a modest compute budget, and a model that beat much larger ones on a lot of benchmarks. Releasing it openly was the most convincing way to make that point, because anyone could verify it.

Now, I'll be honest that it's not purely ideological. Open releases are also how we build trust and distribution. People try the open model, they like it, and then some of them come to us for the larger models, the hosted platform, the enterprise support. So the commercial model and the open model reinforce each other. We don't think we need to release every single thing we train to stay true to the mission, but the default, especially for the models that push efficiency forward, is to put them out there and let people build.

r001.rationale: The response describes rapid community work after Llama’s release, but does not mention university researchers or say they previously lacked access to work on LLMs.

r002.rationale: It says scientific progress comes from people building on one another’s work and gives community improvements to Llama as an example of open releases enabling faster iteration.

r003.rationale: It notes that the most capable systems were behind APIs and argues for inspectability and ownership, but does not identify companies’ unilateral control over who may use those models as a reason to oppose keeping them closed.

astra-6.text:
For us, open source is a way to put the technology into the hands of more people. If you can download a model, run it on your own infrastructure, and adapt it to your needs, you have much more control over what you build. You don’t have to send your data to someone else or depend on a single provider.

It also makes research much more collaborative. People can inspect the models, experiment with them, and find improvements or applications that we wouldn’t have thought of ourselves. We think a small team can do very strong research, but there is far more creativity outside the company than inside it. Making models available lets us benefit from that broader ecosystem while giving people the tools to build on our work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses access to open models generally but does not mention Llama or university researchers who previously lacked access.

r002.rationale: It says open models make research more collaborative and enable people to find improvements, but does not clearly state that shared contributions accelerate scientific progress.

r003.rationale: It mentions avoiding dependence on a single provider, but does not identify companies’ unilateral control over access to the most capable models as a reason to oppose closed models.

sol-6.1.text:
For us, it’s about giving people control over the technology they’re using. If you’re building a product around a language model, you want to be able to understand its capabilities, adapt it to your data, and deploy it on your own infrastructure. You shouldn’t have to send everything to a provider or depend entirely on its decisions.

Open models also allow many more people to experiment and build on each other’s work. We’re a small team; we’re not going to discover every useful application ourselves. Giving developers access to the models lets that ecosystem grow, and we see that as central to what we’re building at Mistral.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention Llama, university researchers, or researchers gaining access to LLMs.

r002.rationale: It says open models let people experiment and build on one another’s work, but does not say this accelerates scientific progress.

r003.rationale: It objects to depending on a provider’s decisions, but does not identify companies’ unilateral control over access to the most capable models as a reason to oppose closed models.
